newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: New World Bank funds expected to protect ecosystems.
newsitem.headline: New World Bank funds expected to protect ecosystems.

text.p: The World Bank will announce $100 million in new funds to protect ecosystems in developing nations at a conference on biological diversity next week, officials said on Friday.

Officials for the World Bank and a leading environmental group said the financing mechanism would ensure swifter action in protecting vital areas like the Amazon by governments under pressure to bolster their conservation programmes.

The bank, one of three implementing agencies for the existing Global Environment Facility (GEF), will announce the new three-year programme here at the third annual conference of the parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity.
Unlike the GEF, which is a cumbersome financing process, these grants would be rushed through in only six months.

"The Bank wants to make grant money available for conserving biodiversity in some of the ecologically most important parts of the world," a member of a leading environmental organisation told Reuters. A World Bank official confirmed the programme will be announced next week.

The Biodiversity Convention, signed at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit, is intended to protect the variety of the world's genes, species and ecosystems, calling for the sustainable use of those resources and the equitable distribution of benefits.
But many complain the convention, ratified by 162 nations, is toothless.

"At the moment of truth, within the convention so far there has not been the willingness to carry out concrete actions," Javier Arreaza, press officer at the Geneva-based World Wide Fund for Nature, told Reuters. "This is an opportunity for the assembly to move from talk to action."
Key themes at the conference are new sources of funding, indigenous rights, genetic engineering and agriculture.

The strongest appeal comes from the world's indigenous groups who are holding their own forum before the conference in a bid to gain recognition of their culture and lifestyles, and of their right to manage their own biological resources. They also seek intellectual property rights.

"The convention cannot be considered separately from the rights of indigenous peoples -- it's not by chance that the main sources of biodiversity are found in our lands," said Max Oof, an Asian delegate to the forum.
Genetic engineering and biological safety standards, drafted at last year's conference in Jakarta, are also expected to stir controversy in the conference.

"Biosafety will be a very hot issue," said Jeffrey McNeely, top biodiversity expert at the Geneva-based World Conservation Union (IUCN), said. "The dilemma we face is: how do we increase productivity and also protect the environment?"
